summary.title: nanoBench: A Low-Overhead Tool for Running Microbenchmarks on x86 Systems
summary.one_liner: nanoBench is a tool for measuring small isolated microbenchmarks with hardware performance counters on Intel and AMD x86 systems, including kernel-space execution, and was used to characterize instruction latencies and cache replacement policies.
keywords: x86 cache replacement policies reverse engineering
takeaways: nanoBench runs small isolated microbenchmarks directly in kernel space, which allows benchmarking privileged instructions and more accurate measurements.
Performance counter reads are implemented with minimal overhead, avoiding function calls and branches, making it precise enough to measure individual memory accesses.
The paper reports using nanoBench to determine latency, throughput, and port usage of more than 13,000 x86 instruction variants.
The paper uses nanoBench-generated microbenchmarks to characterize cache architectures of eleven Intel Core microarchitectures, including cache replacement policies.
summary.summary: This arXiv paper (v2, March 2020) presents nanoBench, a tool for evaluating small, isolated code snippets using hardware performance counters on Intel and AMD x86 systems. Unlike tools that benchmark whole programs or program segments within a larger run, nanoBench can execute microbenchmarks in kernel space, with low-overhead counter reads. The authors illustrate it with two case studies: measuring latency, throughput, and port usage for more than 13,000 instruction variants, and characterizing cache architectures and replacement policies across eleven Intel Core microarchitectures. The listing describes the paper as covering kernel mode with interrupts off, harness overhead removal, and cache replacement policy recovery; the page text itself does not detail those specifics.
